plain_title: When sleep won't come, or won't stay
one_liner: Trouble falling or staying asleep, or waking too early, three nights a week for three months or more.
in_simple_words: Everyone has bad nights. Insomnia disorder is when they become the pattern: lying awake for ages, waking in the night and not getting back off, or waking far too early, several nights a week for months, with tiredness, low mood, and poor concentration by day. It often starts with stress and then gets kept going by worry about sleep itself and by habits that make sense but backfire. It's very common, and the best treatment isn't a pill.
what_it_can_feel_like: Bedtime became the scariest part of the day. The more I tried, the less I slept.
I'd lie there doing maths about how many hours I had left.
CBT for insomnia felt counterintuitive. Less time in bed, more sleep. It worked in six weeks.
common_signs: Taking a long time to fall asleep, or waking and not getting back to sleep
At least three nights a week for three months or more
Tiredness, irritability, low mood, or poor concentration by day
Worrying about sleep and dreading bedtime
Happening even when there's enough time and a decent place to sleep

myths_vs_facts.fact: Sleep needs vary. The problem in insomnia is distress and daytime effects, not a number.
They help short-term but lose effect, cause dependence, and don't fix the pattern. CBT for insomnia works better and lasts.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Lying in bed resting is almost as good as sleep.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Lying awake in bed teaches the brain that bed means wakefulness. Getting up until sleepy is part of the cure.

how_common.plain: About 1 in 10 adults has insomnia disorder, and many more have occasional sleep trouble. Women and older adults are affected more often.
how_common.figure: About 10% of adults (European population estimate); higher rates with broader definitions

what_helps.plain_summary: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended first treatment and works for most people in four to eight sessions, in person, online, or through apps. It resets the link between bed and sleep, tightens the sleep window, and calms worry about sleep. Medication, prescribed and monitored by a doctor, is for short-term use or when CBT-I isn't enough. Treating depression, anxiety, pain, or sleep apnoea often improves insomnia too.
evidence_based_options: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I), including digital versions
Treating co-occurring conditions such as depression, anxiety, pain, or sleep apnoea
Short-term medication in some cases, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
Sleep-restriction and stimulus-control techniques within CBT-I
self_help_that_supports_care: Same wake time every day, even after a bad night
Getting up if awake for more than 20 minutes and returning when sleepy
No clock-watching, and bed only for sleep and sex
Daylight in the morning, less caffeine and alcohol in the evening

when_to_reach_out: If poor sleep has gone on for a month or more and is affecting your days, ask a doctor about CBT for insomnia. Mention snoring, restless legs, or low mood too, as they change the plan.
is_not: A few bad nights during stress, jet lag, shift work, or a new baby aren't insomnia disorder. Sleep trouble caused mainly by sleep apnoea, restless legs, or a body-clock problem is treated differently.
hope_note: Insomnia is one of the most treatable sleep conditions. Most people who complete CBT-I sleep better within weeks and keep the gains.

in_young_people: Teenagers' body clocks run late, so 'insomnia' at 11pm is often biology plus screens. CBT-I works for teens; for younger children, behavioural approaches with parents are used.
across_cultures: Sleep norms differ: co-sleeping, siestas, late dinners, and prayer schedules all shape what's normal. Night-shift and gig work push insomnia rates up in many communities.
